one_liner: Erlang/OTP 29 plus Elixir 1.20 as one Cosmopolitan executable; beats only its own interpreter build, not stock OTP.
what_it_does: Packages ERTS (with the BeamAsm JIT), the OTP applications and Elixir into one Actually Portable Executable that is also a zip; the same ~50 MB file runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD 7.3 on x86_64 and aarch64, reading .beam files from /zip without extracting them. `beam.com INPUT -o OUTPUT` turns a .erl/.ex file, a rebar3 or Mix project, or a `mix release` directory into another single portable executable, and symlinks named mix.com/iex.com/elixir.com act as those tools. A second runtime (ERTS compiled to WebAssembly, npm package beam.com) runs the same app.com on Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy and in browsers. It is a distribution of the Erlang VM, not a library you link.
how_it_is_fast: Nothing in the VM is faster than stock OTP: the speed numbers compare BeamAsm (OTP's own JIT, x86 and arm backends compiled into one fat binary) with the repo's interpreter build of the same code. The only packaging-level speedup is storing kernel and stdlib uncompressed in the zip so the boot reads them without inflating (start of `--version` 193-202 ms to 143-146 ms, local Linux x86_64, interpreter build). Running from the zip in place avoids the unpack-on-first-run step of Burrito and Bakeware.
when_to_use: You want to ship an Erlang or Elixir CLI tool or service as one file that runs on six operating systems and two CPUs with no Erlang install.
Long-running Erlang code on aarch64 (Apple Silicon, ARM servers) where the default JIT build is 3-12x faster than its interpreter build on calls, lists and binaries.
Running a Phoenix or Cowboy app unchanged on Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy or in a browser tab via its WebAssembly runtime.
Short command-line programs where start time matters: use beam-emu.com, which starts 40 to 90 ms faster than the JIT build.
when_not_to_use: As a faster Erlang VM: there is no measurement against stock Erlang/OTP, and several build choices (below) make parts of it slower than a normal OTP install.
TLS- or crypto-heavy services: OpenSSL 4.0.3 is built with no-asm, so the crypto NIF runs portable C code; the bench's SHA-256 of 64 MB takes 237-254 ms, about 260 MB/s (derived from page data).
Servers with many concurrent sockets: ERTS is configured with --disable-kernel-poll and the select() backend (no epoll or kqueue), capped at FD_SETSIZE, and without the socket NIF (--disable-esock).
Projects that need native NIFs or drivers from shared objects, git dependencies, umbrella projects, config/runtime.exs, run_erl, port programs on Windows, or OpenBSD 7.4 and later.
Production use where maturity counts: 0 stars, one maintainer, first release candidates (v0.1.0-rc.2), and the Cosmopolitan fd-table races it had to patch around.

integration.form: single prebuilt executable (APE); also an npm package for the WebAssembly runtime
integration.dependencies: none at run time (Erlang/OTP 29.1.1, Elixir 1.20.4, OpenSSL 4.0.3, SQLite via esqlite, WAMR and Cosmopolitan Libc are linked in); building it needs cosmocc 4.0.2
integration.min_toolchain: none to run; build: cosmocc 4.0.2 (GCC-based), OTP CFLAGS -O2 -g, SQLite -Os; Node.js 25+ or Deno 2.9 for the WebAssembly runtime (JSPI)
integration.platforms: Linux x86_64/aarch64 (and WSL2), macOS arm64/x86_64, Windows x86_64 (no port programs), FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD 7.3 via the APE loader; Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy, browsers with JSPI
integration.thread_safety: standard ERTS SMP schedulers; BEAM.com wraps Cosmopolitan close() under the fd-table lock to fix two races (C25, C26 in docs/UPSTREAM.md) that broke about 1 in 100 busy starts and crashed some builds
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — runs unmodified Erlang/Elixir code and releases built for OTP 29.1.1, but not native NIF .so files, the socket module, kernel poll or Windows port programs

gotchas: Not unmodified OTP: two patches plus configure overrides (select() poll backend, no esock, no sendfile, no Linux THP alignment, --disable-security-hardening-flags, zstd without assembly, and the JIT built without the native stack on x86_64 too, where stock OTP enables it).
The headline aarch64 gains (fib 139 to 12 ms, about 11.6x) are JIT against an interpreter the docs call slow (fib 2-3x slower than on x86_64); they say nothing about stock OTP's JIT or interpreter.

Harness: bench.erl times each workload with timer:tc rounded down to whole ms, best of 3, on shared CI runners with about 10% noise and no CPU model; the start rows take the 5th of 10 sorted runs and include the sh launcher; the first local table compares an x86_64-only interpreter file with the fat JIT file; the performance gate compares a PR only with the edge build of main.

The WebAssembly runtime runs Erlang code at 1.2-1.4x the time of the native interpreter in Node.js and 25-30% slower again in workerd; on Cloudflare the clock does not move during work, so timer:tc gives no CPU time there.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued siblings runs Erlang: they are Wasm and EVM engines, and BEAM.com only embeds WAMR as its Wasm interpreter (no Wasm JIT, no SIMD), so use WAMR or Wasmi directly for WebAssembly. Pick BEAM.com over Burrito or Bakeware when you want one file for every OS and CPU with no unpack step, and over a normal OTP install only for distribution convenience, never for speed.
verified_claims_summary: docs/BENCHMARKS.md compares the repo's own JIT build (beam.com) with its interpreter build (beam-emu.com), both cosmocc 4.0.2 at -O2, on shared CI runners and a 4-CPU Linux x86_64 box with no CPU model: Linux x86_64 fib(32) 70 to 30 ms, lists 249 to 116, binary 249 to 133, messages 111 to 117 (no gain), start 142 to 222 ms (slower); Linux aarch64 fib 139 to 12 ms. Storing kernel and stdlib uncompressed cut start from 193-202 ms to 143-146 ms against its own all-compressed variant; nothing is measured against stock Erlang/OTP.
status_note: Very active (511 commits, last commit 2026-10-06, release candidate v0.1.0-rc.2) and Apache-2.0 with bundled third-party licences, but a single-maintainer project with 0 stars whose value is portable packaging, not speed.
